3cf482741f.q: What is Ocean Youth Trust South and how does it work with young people?
3cf482741f.a: Ocean Youth Trust South is a charity that takes young people aged 12 to 25 to sea through sail training voyages aboard their vessel. They work with about 600 young people a year with the support of about 70 volunteers, and their work combines sailing instruction (including RYA start yachting and competent crew certificates) with youth development focusing on teamwork, communication skills, and resilience. The charity operates as an outdoor residential experience afloat, teaching practical skills while also addressing mental wellbeing and building community.

ks: Ocean Youth Trust South takes approximately 600 young people to sea per year
The charity operates with about 70 volunteers and 8 sea staff at a time (2-3 paid staff, 5 volunteers)
The Prolific vessel main mast is 30 metres high, requiring teams of 10 people to pull the main sail up
The mizzen sail requires 8 people to pull up
The previous boat was 22 metres in length and 55 gross tons; Prolific is 32 metres with 114 gross tons (double the volume)
3cf482741f.gt: Chief Executive at Ocean Youth Trust South

f4a64054f5.q: How does Ocean Youth Trust South support young people's mental wellbeing according to the five steps framework?
f4a64054f5.a: Ocean Youth Trust South incorporates the five steps to wellbeing identified by Your Mind into their voyages: connect (building friendships and family-like bonds through shared meals and experiences), be active (pulling ropes and working the boat, such as the 30-metre high main mast requiring teams of 10 people), and take notice (observing the natural world around them, such as seeing the Milky Way for the first time or watching dolphins and eclipses). These elements provide young people with life-changing experiences and lasting memories that build their confidence and sense of achievement.

95ab231aca.q: What career opportunities have young people achieved after sailing with Ocean Youth Trust South?
95ab231aca.a: Several young people who sailed with Ocean Youth Trust South have gone on to significant careers, including one who became dockmaster at MDL Marinas and Ocean Village, and another who attended Dartmouth Naval College after leading a group of visually impaired young people on a voyage and now works on the Queen Elizabeth. Some participants also pursue careers within the yachting industry through obtaining their sailing certifications during voyages.

ff7546a26b.q: How did Mark Todd transition from being a lawyer to leading Ocean Youth Trust South?
ff7546a26b.a: Mark Todd studied law and psychology at university and practiced commercial and personal injury law for approximately five years, heading a personal injury department. He became disillusioned with the administrative demands of legal practice and took up sailing as a hobby, eventually volunteering with Ocean Youth Club for six months to gain training and refitting experience. He was offered the Boson's job at £70 per week and began sailing with young people, which he describes as absolutely incredible, leading him to stay 27 years ago and never look back.

eaa75777f0.q: What were the major financial and operational challenges Ocean Youth Trust South faced in its early years?
eaa75777f0.a: Ocean Youth Trust South faced significant financial difficulties in its early years, with the organisation being on the brink of financial collapse. Additionally, upgrading from their previous 22-metre, 55 gross ton boat to their current vessel, the Prolific—a 32-metre, 114 gross ton boat—required approximately half a million pounds in refurbishment costs, which represented a substantial financial strain for a charity with limited staff resources.
